text: Halter, the New Zealand startup whose solar-powered GPS collars let cattle be herded and fenced without wire, raised $220 million in a Series E round in March 2026 that valued the company at $2 billion — double its roughly $1 billion price from nine months earlier. The round was led by Peter Thiel's Founders Fund, the same firm that backed Halter's first $8 million raise back in 2018. Founder Craig Piggott built the "cowgorithm" — Halter's internal name for the software that decides how and when to nudge an animal — after leaving an engineering job at Rocket Lab, where his boss, founder Peter Beck, later became one of Halter's earliest backers and a board member. Eight years and five funding rounds later, Halter is one of the best-capitalized private companies to come out of New Zealand and arguably the best-funded startup in the small, real category of livestock virtual fencing — and its $2 billion price tag now puts it on the Unicorn Tracker alongside far more crowded categories. Figures compiled from Bloomberg, Businesswire, AgFunderNews, and Halter's own March 2026 funding announcement. Total funding is a cumulative estimate across five disclosed rounds; exact currency conversions (NZD/AUD to USD) vary slightly by source. Halter Valuation 2026: From $1 Billion to $2 Billion in Nine Months Halter's valuation went from roughly $1 billion in June 2025 to roughly $2 billion in March 2026 — a doubling in nine months, confirmed by the company and reported by Bloomberg and Businesswire. The March 2026 round raised $220 million (reported as NZ$377 million in New Zealand press and roughly A$314.5 million in Australian coverage — all figures for the same USD-denominated raise), one of the largest single rounds in agtech history according to AgFunderNews. The jump follows a pattern of accelerating rounds rather than one big leap: Halter took nine years to reach its first $1 billion valuation and then just nine months to add a second billion, a timeline the company itself has highlighted. Founders Fund led the new round, with existing backers Blackbird, DCVC, Bond, Bessemer Venture Partners, NewView, Ubiquity, and Icehouse Ventures all returning. How a Cow-Collar Company Actually Makes Money Halter runs a subscription model, not a one-time hardware sale. Farmers pay from NZ$9.90 (about US$5.70) per cow per month for the collar and software, on top of a one-time infrastructure cost of roughly NZ$7,800 per base-station tower — each tower covers an area with an effective radius of about 8 kilometers, depending on terrain. That pricing structure is why Halter and its backers describe the business as recurring software revenue with hardware attached, rather than a farm-equipment sale. Halter does not publish revenue, but third-party estimates from the investing newsletter New Market Pitch put annual recurring revenue somewhere in the $70 million to $100 million range, based on roughly 1 million collars at typical subscription rates. On that estimate, a $2 billion valuation implies a revenue multiple in the neighborhood of 20x to 28x ARR — rich for a hardware-adjacent business, but not unusual for 2026-era venture pricing of a company growing collar count as fast as Halter has. The Market Halter Is Betting Its $2 Billion On The broader category Halter competes in — AI-driven virtual fencing and smart livestock management — was valued at roughly $1.8 billion globally in 2025 and is projected to reach $7.89 billion by 2034, a 17.5% compound annual growth rate, according to InsightAce Analytic. A narrower estimate focused specifically on virtual fencing for livestock puts that segment at $325 million in 2024, growing to $1.27 billion by 2033 at a 16.5% CAGR. Either way, Halter's $2 billion private valuation is already larger than the entire addressable market it competes in today, which is exactly the bet growth investors are making: that the category itself is still early and will expand several times over as traditional wire and electric fencing get replaced. That bet has some real-world grounding. Virtual fencing solves a problem that has nothing to do with novelty: physical fencing on large cattle operations is expensive to install, expensive to repair after storms or fallen trees, and inflexible when a farmer wants to change pasture rotation for grazing management. Halter's own materials point to farmers using its rotational-grazing tools to increase pasture utilization and reduce the labor hours spent moving herds by hand — the kind of operational savings that make a $5.70-per-cow-per-month subscription an easier sell than the sticker price alone suggests. Whether that translates into the revenue growth needed to justify a 20x-plus ARR multiple is the open question the next 12 to 18 months of Halter's US expansion will answer. The Founders Fund Connection: Same Investor, Eight Years Apart Craig Piggott grew up on a Waikato dairy farm, studied mechanical engineering with first-class honors at the University of Auckland, and then took an engineering job at Rocket Lab under founder Peter Beck before starting Halter in 2016 at age 21. Beck became an early investor, joined Halter's board, and helped bring in the roughly $8 million Series A in 2018 — a round that also included Peter Thiel's Founders Fund. Founders Fund's return to lead the $220 million Series E eight years later is a meaningful signal in a market where seed investors rarely have enough conviction — or enough capital reserved — to lead a company's growth-stage round. It also puts Halter in company with other Founders Fund-backed New Zealand and Pacific deep-tech bets, reinforcing the firm's pattern of writing early checks into unusual, capital-intensive hardware-plus-software companies and staying in for the long run rather than rotating out after the seed stage.
